names: Union Iron Works Foundry and Warehouse
summary: The 1885-86 brick Machine Shop and blacksmith/boiler shop (113/114, joined by a 1914 concrete connector, 492 ft long), which the NRHP calls the earliest remaining building in the district, and the 1916-17 reinforced-concrete foundry and warehouse (115/116) beside it. Building 113/114 was closed by the Port and red-tagged in 2001 (115/116 was used for storage). Both were rehabilitated by Orton Development with a buckling-restrained-brace steel system and public atrium, receiving certificates of occupancy in November 2017 (115/116) and April 2018 (113/114), and were subleased to Uber Advanced Technologies Group and Gusto. The state's Office of Historic Preservation lists the 'Historic Shipyard at Pier 70 Rehabilitation' of the '20th Street Historic Buildings at Pier 70' among its 2023 Governor's Historic Preservation Awards; its statement does not name individual buildings, but the Historic Preservation Commission's 2013 packet includes Buildings 113 to 116 in that group.

milestones.text: Eastern portion of Building 113/114 (blacksmith and boiler shop) completed to civil engineer D. E. Melliss's design; western portion (machine shop) completed 1886 (NRHP, STRUCTURE magazine and the Port's Table 1 give 1885/1886; the Port memo's text and the 2013 Historic Preservation Commission packet also say 'built from 1885-1888')
The two brick buildings joined by a reinforced concrete and steel connector
Contract of almost $100,000 awarded for the new one-story reinforced concrete foundry (Building 115), under construction by June 1916; Bethlehem's plans date 115/116 to 1917
Machine shop closed by the Port and red-tagged for its hazardous unreinforced-masonry condition, after use for ship repair until then
Port Commission endorses the Pier 70 Preferred Master Plan (Resolution 10-27), which calls for a National Register district and rehabilitation of the 20th Street buildings

Port Commission awards the 20th Street Historic Buildings opportunity to Orton Development after a 2011 RFP; Exclusive Negotiating Agreement approved April 2012; term sheet endorsed October 2012 (Board of Supervisors December 2012)

Historic Preservation Commission informational packet (memo dated Nov 26, 2013; the hearing date is not stated in the packet) on the rehabilitation of the ten 20th Street Historic Buildings (case 2013.1168E): ~270,000 gsf existing plus ~69,000 gsf of new mezzanines, ~334,000 gsf total
Union Iron Works Historic District listed in the National Register of Historic Places (NRIS 14000150), giving the project access to federal historic tax credits
Port Commission Resolution 14-33 approves the Lease Disposition and Development Agreement and 66-year Master Lease (L-15814) with Historic Pier 70, LLC (Orton) and adopts CEQA findings

Master lease approved by the Board of Supervisors and fully executed, giving Orton site control; the Port's January 2019 memo says construction commenced thereafter. The National Trust (Winter 2016 issue) says the rehabilitation 'began this past September' without printing the year, which would be September 2015, while Bisnow (April 2017) says Orton began the redevelopment 'in 2014'; the sources do not agree on the start year
Permanent financing for the Historic Core project achieved

Port staff update to the Commission (memo dated Jan 4, 2019): six of eight buildings complete, Buildings 101 and 102 still under construction, project 100% subleased except two atrium retail spaces; whole-Historic-Core project total costs (not the cost of this building alone) rose from $81.9M at 2014 approvals to $127.0M in Table 2's '2018, Actual' column, while the memo's text gives 'an estimated $125 million at project completion in 2020'; Table 2 marks one line (Building 102's $6.7M) as a future-expenditure estimate
Historic Shipyard at Pier 70 Rehabilitation receives a Governor's Historic Preservation Award

Two magnitude-4.0 earthquakes shake the Bay Area in summer 2015 while Building 113, constructed in 1885, is already described as on the verge of collapse; the National Trust's Winter 2016 issue says the building 'has since been stabilized' but gives no date for the stabilization
Gusto sublease of Building 113 East (49,074 sq ft) commences, ten years, office

Bisnow reports that Orton signed a 130,000 sq ft lease with Uber-owned Otto, a self-driving truck company, and that Historic Pier 70 is then '85% leased' (the Bisnow article's date is a report date, not the lease date)
Certificate of occupancy for Buildings 115/116; Uber Advanced Technologies Group sublease of Buildings 114, 115 and 116 (79,771 sq ft, ten years, PDR) commences
Uber Advanced Technologies Group sublease of Building 113 West (51,299 sq ft, two years, office) commences
Certificate of occupancy for Buildings 113/114
Two small retail spaces in the Building 113 atrium still available; Orton begins activating the atrium and plaza with events

costs.what: Hard cost of the Building 113/114 rehabilitation (2018 actual; $24.2M for 113 and 114 combined at 2014 approvals)
Hard cost of the Building 115/116 rehabilitation (2018 actual; $7.1M combined at 2014 approvals)
Contract for the new foundry (Building 115) in January 1916 ('almost $100,000')

facts.value: Orton Development, Inc. through Historic Pier 70, LLC (66-year master lease L-15814 from the Port of San Francisco)
Marcy Wong Donn Logan Architects and Mark Hulbert Preservation Architecture, named by STRUCTURE magazine among the Building 113/114 project team (the article gives no roles)
Nabih Youssef Structural Engineers, named by STRUCTURE magazine among the Building 113/114 project team

Developer equity up to $14 million plus loans; Port participation rent of 50% of revenues above debt and a 14% equity return; sources in 2018: Port capital $1.8M, Seismic Safety Loan $23.6M, historic tax credit equity $20.4M, private debt and equity $81.2M
Contributing resource to the Union Iron Works Historic District (NRHP, listed April 17, 2014)
Dr. D. E. Melliss, civil engineer (113/114); designer of 115/116 not recorded
113/114: 492 ft by 175 ft 6 in by 62 ft tall; 115/116: 218 ft by 174 ft by 57 ft 2 in
113/114: 89,686 (NRHP), 95,157 before and 129,228 after rehabilitation (Port); 115/116: 33,858 (NRHP), 38,694 before and 53,625 after (Port)

New perimeter steel framing at two levels stabilizes the unreinforced brick walls (up to 18 inches out of plumb); buckling-restrained braced frames provide lateral resistance; new interior steel frame and mezzanines
Office and PDR (113/114); PDR (115/116); 'New American Workplace' light-industrial definition with ancillary office, showroom and retail
Uber Advanced Technologies Group (113 West, 114, 115, 116) and Gusto (113 East) per the Port's January 2019 sublease list; STRUCTURE later describes 'two technology tenants'
Building 113-114 atrium (the 1914 connector) and the ~45,000 sq ft plaza framed with Building 14 are publicly accessible under Master Lease Exhibit K

The 2013 Historic Preservation Commission packet says Buildings 23 and 24, minor appendages on the east end of Building 113 totaling about 1,500 gsf, 'would be demolished' to facilitate rehabilitation (the NRHP dates Building 23 to 1941 and Building 24 to 1914, upgraded in 1936 and 1941); none of the sources read confirms they were removed

Built as the Union Iron Works' machine, blacksmith and boiler shops; the Building 115 foundry produced over a million pounds of castings a month by 1919; 'Pacific Coast Steel Corporation' lettering survives on 115/116

open_questions: Current tenants: Uber ATG's Building 113 West sublease was a two-year term from February 2018, and WPXI reported on January 20, 2021 that Aurora had closed its acquisition of Uber's self-driving unit (the deal announced in December 2020); no source confirms who occupies 113 West, 114-116 or 113 East today.
The STRUCTURE magazine article is undated on the page; it describes the project as 'currently complete', so it post-dates April 2018.
This record covers both Assessor-lot groupings (the retired lot 4111004 is not mapped as a record of its own); the geometry is the D4D's single 113-116 box.

Construction start: the Port's January 2019 memo says construction followed the July 2015 execution of the master lease, the National Trust (Winter 2016 issue) says the rehabilitation 'began this past September' (the year is not printed), and Bisnow (April 2017) says Orton began the redevelopment 'in 2014'. No source read settles the start year.
Buildings 23 and 24 on the east end of Building 113: the 2013 plan said they would be demolished; no source read confirms whether they were removed.
